The window seat on the 7:14 was never empty, except that Tuesday when it was. I hesitated in the aisle, my hand on the damp rail, as if the empty seat had been left by a ghost. Rain pearled on the window and the city beyond smeared into watercolor. I sat.

Across from me, a man held a paper cup with both hands like it was a small animal. He was talking to no one, or to someone on the phone, but I saw no earbuds. His lips moved with the rhythm of a prayer. I tried not to stare. The train lurched, and a little coffee sloshed onto his thumb. He didn't react.

I thought about how we are all just carrying small animals—coffee cups, grudges, the memory of someone's voice—and how the train doesn't care. The conductor's voice crackled, announcing a delay. A woman beside me sighed, a long, theatrical exhale that smelled of mint and resignation. She pulled a book from her bag, its spine cracked like a dry riverbed. I caught the title: "A Field Guide to Vanishing Things." I almost asked her if it was any good, but the question felt too intimate for 7:18 in the morning.

Instead, I looked out the window. There was a billboard I'd passed a hundred times, advertising a furniture store that had closed years ago. The sign was faded, but at a certain angle the sun hit it and for a second it looked new. I used to think that was sad. Now I thought it was a kind of honesty: everything fades, but sometimes the light forgives it.

The man across from me stood abruptly. He left his cup on the seat. It tilted, spilled a brown crescent onto the blue fabric, and he walked toward the doors without looking back. The train was stopped between stations, but he stood at the door, his reflection a dark shape against the rain. No one said anything. The woman with the book glanced up, then back down. I felt a sudden, irrational urge to follow him, to ask what he had been praying about. But the doors weren't open. There was nowhere to go.

That's the thing about trains: they hold you in the in-between. You are neither where you left nor where you're going. You are suspended, and in that suspension, the smallest gestures become enormous. A man leaving a coffee cup. A woman sighing. The way the rain makes the city look like a memory of itself.

I remembered a conversation I'd had with my father years ago. We were driving, not on a train, and he said, "You know, everyone is fighting a battle you can't see." I had rolled my eyes then, sixteen and invincible. But now, watching the man at the door, I thought maybe my father had been right. The man's battle was written in the set of his shoulders, in the way he didn't wipe the coffee from his hand. It was not my battle to understand, but it was mine to witness.

The train lurched forward. The doors stayed closed. The man remained standing, his hand on the pole, his body swaying with the motion. I watched the back of his head, the way his hair curled just above his collar. He was maybe forty, maybe sixty. Time had not been kind to him, or maybe it had been too kind, leaving him soft around the edges.

The woman next to me closed her book. She turned to me and said, "Do you ever think about how many people you've sat next to and never known?" Her voice was low, as if she were continuing a conversation we'd been having for years.

I blinked. "All the time," I said, though I hadn't until that moment.

She nodded. "I think that's why I read field guides. They make the unknown seem catalogued. But people aren't like that. You can't flip to the back and find their name."

I wanted to say something profound, but the train stopped again and the doors opened with a pneumatic hiss. The man stepped off. I watched him walk down the platform, his figure dissolving into the gray. The woman stood, too. She tucked her book into her bag and gave me a small smile, the kind you give a stranger when you've shared something you can't name.

"Have a good life," she said, and then she was gone.

I sat there for a moment, the empty seat beside me now holding only the ghost of her mint breath. I thought about what she said. Have a good life. Not "have a good day." It was such an odd, generous thing to say to a stranger. It acknowledged the asymmetry of our paths—that we would likely never see each other again, but that our lives were still happening, full and parallel.

The train moved on. The rain had stopped. Sunlight broke through the clouds and lit the empty coffee cup on the seat across from me. It was still there, a small monument to the man's departure. I wondered if he'd ever think about the cup. Probably not. But I would think about it for a long time, the way we hold on to the things that don't belong to us.

At my stop, I stood and walked to the doors. The platform was slick with rain, and the air smelled like wet concrete and exhaust. I stepped off and into the city, which was waking up despite everything. People rushed past, their faces lit by phone screens, their steps purposeful. I felt slow among them, like I was still moving at the speed of the train.

I went inside. I pressed my floor and watched the numbers climb. Somewhere, someone was praying; somewhere else, a woman was reading about vanishing things. And I was in between, carrying my small animal, trying to remember that everyone is always fighting a battle I can't see.

The window seat on the 7:14 was never empty, except that Tuesday when it was. I hesitated in the aisle, my hand on the damp rail, as if the empty seat had been left by a ghost. Rain pearled on the window and the city beyond smeared into watercolor. I sat.

Across from me, a man held a paper cup with both hands like it was a small animal. He was talking to no one, or to someone on the phone, but I saw no earbuds. His lips moved with the rhythm of a prayer. I tried not to stare. The train lurched, and a little coffee sloshed onto his thumb. He didn't react.

I thought about how we are all just carrying small animals—coffee cups, grudges, the memory of someone's voice—and how the train doesn't care. The conductor's voice crackled, announcing a delay. A woman beside me sighed, a long, theatrical exhale that smelled of mint and resignation. She pulled a book from her bag, its spine cracked like a dry riverbed. I caught the title: "A Field Guide to Vanishing Things." I almost asked her if it was any good, but the question felt too intimate for 7:18 in the morning.

Instead, I looked out the window. There was a billboard I'd passed a hundred times, advertising a furniture store that had closed years ago. The sign was faded, but at a certain angle the sun hit it and for a second it looked new. I used to think that was sad. Now I thought it was a kind of honesty: everything fades, but sometimes the light forgives it.

The man across from me stood abruptly. He left his cup on the seat. It tilted, spilled a brown crescent onto the blue fabric, and he walked toward the doors without looking back. The train was stopped between stations, but he stood at the door, his reflection a dark shape against the rain. No one said anything. The woman with the book glanced up, then back down. I felt a sudden, irrational urge to follow him, to ask what he had been praying about. But the doors weren't open. There was nowhere to go.

That's the thing about trains: they hold you in the in-between. You are neither where you left nor where you're going. You are suspended, and in that suspension, the smallest gestures become enormous. A man leaving a coffee cup. A woman sighing. The way the rain makes the city look like a memory of itself.

I remembered a conversation I'd had with my father years ago. We were driving, not on a train, and he said, "You know, everyone is fighting a battle you can't see." I had rolled my eyes then, sixteen and invincible. But now, watching the man at the door, I thought maybe my father had been right. The man's battle was written in the set of his shoulders, in the way he didn't wipe the coffee from his hand. It was not my battle to understand, but it was mine to witness.

The train lurched forward. The doors stayed closed. The man remained standing, his hand on the pole, his body swaying with the motion. I watched the back of his head, the way his hair curled just above his collar. He was maybe forty, maybe sixty. Time had not been kind to him, or maybe it had been too kind, leaving him soft around the edges.

The woman next to me closed her book. She turned to me and said, "Do you ever think about how many people you've sat next to and never known?" Her voice was low, as if she were continuing a conversation we'd been having for years.

I blinked. "All the time," I said, though I hadn't until that moment.

She nodded. "I think that's why I read field guides. They make the unknown seem catalogued. But people aren't like that. You can't flip to the back and find their name."

I wanted to say something profound, but the train stopped again and the doors opened with a pneumatic hiss. The man stepped off. I watched him walk down the platform, his figure dissolving into the gray. The woman stood, too. She tucked her book into her bag and gave me a small smile, the kind you give a stranger when you've shared something you can't name.

"Have a good life," she said, and then she was gone.

I sat there for a moment, the empty seat beside me now holding only the ghost of her mint breath. I thought about what she said. Have a good life. Not "have a good day." It was such an odd, generous thing to say to a stranger. It acknowledged the asymmetry of our paths—that we would likely never see each other again, but that our lives were still happening, full and parallel.

The train moved on. The rain had stopped. Sunlight broke through the clouds and lit the empty coffee cup on the seat across from me. It was still there, a small monument to the man's departure. I wondered if he'd ever think about the cup. Probably not. But I would think about it for a long time, the way we hold on to the things that don't belong to us.

At my stop, I stood and walked to the doors. The platform was slick with rain, and the air smelled like wet concrete and exhaust. I stepped off and into the city, which was waking up despite everything. People rushed past, their faces lit by phone screens, their steps purposeful. I felt slow among them, like I was still moving at the speed of the train.

I went inside. I pressed my floor and watched the numbers climb. Somewhere, someone was praying; somewhere else, a woman was reading about vanishing things. And I was in between, carrying my small animal, trying to remember that everyone is always fighting a battle I can't see.
